summary:
Zacatecas operates a legislated route to legal gender recognition. On 23 December 2022 deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code of Zacatecas on gender identity by 14 votes to 7, after the Justice Committee had issued a positive opinion, establishing the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community.

Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature records the same reform as an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and adds that in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the law; both entries link to the official state gazette. In the Human Rights Watch count of 31 March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and six had enacted none — Zacatecas is not among the states lacking one.

A protective criminal-law floor applies in the state. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a ban on conversion therapies, or ECOSIG (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género), by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code, penalising with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code.

The document route arrived later than the protective criminal law: the gender-identity initiative debated alongside the 2021 session, which proposed constitutional and Family Code reform, failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at that time, passing only in December 2022.
tangentialFactors:
The national picture frames what Zacatecas offers. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure and named six whose legislatures had enacted none, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Delays and refusals elsewhere in the country carry documented consequences. Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 found that in Tabasco, name and gender recognition delays leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence risk is a standing national concern. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009.
localsOnly:
Residents of Zacatecas may apply for a new birth certificate recognising their gender identity under the December 2022 Family Code reform, with the state Civil Registry's 2023 guidelines setting out how the administrative procedure is run.

State residents are covered by the Penal Code provisions of 25 August 2021: article 182 Bis fraction VI punishes incitement to hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and the promotion of conversion practices, with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work, and hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity are typified in the same code.

Residents seeking recognition elsewhere in the country face uneven provision: 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a procedure by March 2025, and delays in states without a functioning route leave people carrying documents that contradict their lived identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state what the Zacatecas procedure requires of applicants — whether a diagnosis, surgery, sterilisation or court appearance is a precondition, or what fees and timelines apply. The official state gazette links carried by Human Rights Watch would be the place to verify this.

Unresolved: no sourced record of any enforcement action under article 182 Bis fraction VI, or of any completed prosecution for a hate crime typified in August 2021, appears in the inventory. The existence of the provisions is documented; their application is not.

Unresolved: the inventory does not specify whether Zacatecas's hate-crime typification carries an enhanced penalty, nor whether the state has any separate provision on transfemicide comparable to Mexico City's Paola Buenrostro law of July 2024.

Not sourced: no data specific to Zacatecas on killings or attacks against trans people is included here; the violence figures cited are national or international.
